summary.text: Take the counterexample \(N=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), whose three prime-power factors are pairwise coprime. Using \(a(n)=2\sigma(n)-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\) and multiplicativity of both terms gives \(\sigma(N)=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010=66183576284700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011=132367152569399\), so \(a(N)=1\) although \(N\ne1,12\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e
\]
denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency used in the definition of A296075 is
\[
\delta(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
and hence
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\delta(d)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

Take
\[
N=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009.
\]
We first record that the two displayed odd factors really are distinct primes. This can be checked compactly by the following standard order criterion: if \(M>1\), the complete prime factorization of \(M-1\) is known, and an integer \(b\) satisfies
\[
b^{M-1}\equiv1\pmod M
\]
together with
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(M-1)/q}-1,M\bigr)=1
\]
for every prime \(q\mid M-1\), then \(M\) is prime. Indeed, if \(r\) is any prime divisor of \(M\), the first congruence makes the order of \(b\) modulo \(r\) divide \(M-1\). For each prime power \(q^e\) exactly dividing \(M-1\), the gcd condition for \(q\) shows that this order cannot divide \((M-1)/q\), so its \(q\)-adic exponent is \(e\). Thus the order is exactly \(M-1\). Since the order also divides \(r-1\), one has \(M-1\mid r-1\), and therefore \(r\ge M\). As \(r\mid M\), this forces \(r=M\), proving that \(M\) is prime.

For \(4409\), we have
\[
4409-1=4408=2^3\cdot19\cdot29.
\]
The numbers \(19\) and \(29\) are prime (division by primes no larger than their square roots suffices: for \(19\), test \(2,3\), and for \(29\), test \(2,3,5\)). With base \(b=3\), repeated squaring gives
\[
3^{4408}\equiv1\pmod{4409},
\]
and the residues needed for the three distinct prime divisors of \(4408\) are
\[
3^{2204}\equiv4408,
\qquad
3^{232}\equiv209,
\qquad
3^{152}\equiv3965
\pmod{4409}.
\]
Their differences from \(1\) have gcd \(1\) with \(4409\):
\[
\gcd(4407,4409)=\gcd(208,4409)=\gcd(3964,4409)=1.
\]
The criterion therefore proves that \(4409\) is prime.

For the other factor,
\[
458009-1=458008=2^3\cdot57251.
\]
We also need the primality of \(57251\). Its predecessor factors as
\[
57251-1=57250=2\cdot5^3\cdot229,
\]
and \(229\) is prime: its square root is less than \(16\), and it is divisible by none of \(2,3,5,7,11,13\). For base \(2\), repeated squaring modulo \(57251\) gives
\[
2^{57250}\equiv1\pmod{57251}
\]
and
\[
2^{28625}\equiv57250,
\qquad
2^{11450}\equiv55371,
\qquad
2^{250}\equiv48088
\pmod{57251}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\gcd(57249,57251)=\gcd(55370,57251)=\gcd(48087,57251)=1.
\]
These correspond respectively to the distinct prime divisors \(2,5,229\) of \(57250\), so the order criterion proves that \(57251\) is prime.

Now use base \(3\) modulo \(458009\). Repeated squaring gives
\[
3^{458008}\equiv1\pmod{458009},
\]
and, for the distinct prime factors \(2\) and \(57251\) of \(458008\),
\[
3^{229004}\equiv458008,
\qquad
3^8\equiv6561
\pmod{458009}.
\]
Here
\[
\gcd(458007,458009)=1,
\qquad
\gcd(6560,458009)=1.
\]
Thus the same criterion proves that \(458009\) is prime. In particular, \(2^{14}\), \(4409\), and \(458009\) are pairwise coprime.

We next reduce the sequence value to two ordinary divisor sums. Distributing the sum in the definition gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
 &=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
 &=2\sigma(n)-S(n),
\end{aligned}
\]
where for convenience we set
\[
S(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Both \(\sigma\) and \(S\) are multiplicative on coprime arguments. Here is the direct reason. If \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime, every divisor of \(mn\) has a unique expression \(uv\), where \(u\mid m\) and \(v\mid n\). Consequently
\[
\sigma(mn)=\sum_{u\mid m}\sum_{v\mid n}uv
=\left(\sum_{u\mid m}u\right)\left(\sum_{v\mid n}v\right)
=\sigma(m)\sigma(n).
\]
Using the same unique factorization of divisors, together with the just-proved multiplicativity of \(\sigma\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(mn)
 &=\sum_{u\mid m}\sum_{v\mid n}\sigma(uv)\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid m}\sum_{v\mid n}\sigma(u)\sigma(v)\\
 &=S(m)S(n).
\end{aligned}
\]

For a prime \(p\), the divisors of \(p^k\) are \(1,p,\ldots,p^k\), so
\[
\sigma(p^k)=1+p+\cdots+p^k
\]
and
\[
S(p^k)=\sum_{j=0}^k\sigma(p^j)
       =\sum_{j=0}^k\sum_{i=0}^j p^i.
\]
Applying these formulas to \(2^{14}\) yields
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767.
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}(1+2+\cdots+2^j)\\
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}(2^{j+1}-1)\\
 &=2(2^{15}-1)-15\\
 &=65519.
\end{aligned}
\]
For a prime occurring to the first power, the corresponding formulas simplify to
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1,
\qquad
S(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 x & \sigma(x)&S(x)\\ \hline
 2^{14}&32767&65519\\
 4409&4410&4411\\
 458009&458010&458011.
\end{array}
\]

Since these three factors are pairwise coprime, multiplicativity now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010\\
 &=66183576284700,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(N)
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011\\
 &=132367152569399.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\sigma(N)-S(N)\\
 &=2\cdot66183576284700-132367152569399\\
 &=132367152569400-132367152569399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally,
\[
N=33085221781504
\]
is plainly neither \(1\) nor \(12\). Thus there is a positive integer \(N\notin\{1,12\}\) with \(a(N)=1\). This counterexample disproves the assertion that, for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\).
